name: Bukar Sadong
catalog_quote: Simple words in Mentu Land Dayak have one, two, three or four syllables; the last syllable of a polysyllabic word behaves in the same way as as the only syllable in a monosyllabic word and phonetically is stressed. [...] In polysyllabic words the first syllable allows more vowel contrasts than any word-medial syllables and may be considered to have secondary stress (not indicated).
sweep_summary: Two sweep items, both the same paper: Rensch 'Rhythm in Bidayuh' as a 2006 10-ICAL preprint (Glottolog 95762; print-only — SPLC 19 contents page recovered from Wayback and saved, but no PDF of the published version exists on the SIL Philippines online list, SIL Global record 51516 is 404/503, no Wayback capture). The paper is about ultima vowel length and full/reduced penult vowels, with one stress sentence (p.2): 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation' — confirms the catalog's fixed-strict final-stress coding for Bukar-Sadung (Eastern Bidayuh). The more authoritative first-hand statement read in this sweep is Rensch et al. 2012 (SIL e-Book 33,: p.47 ultima receives the peak of word stress in citation forms, p.94 fn.79 enclitics take the stress, p.292 Land Dayak consistently accents the final syllable of the stem. Nothing read contradicts or refines the coding; it does not supersede the catalog's deciding source (Court 1972 via StressTyp2, the lect-specific phonology, still print-only). searching was done by direct fetches (SIL Philippines, Wayback, Crossref, Glottolog).

new_statements.quote: "In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually)." [p.47] — "Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached." [p.94 fn.79] — "They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position." [p.292, of the Land Dayak languages]
new_statements.citation: Rensch, Calvin R., Carolyn M. Rensch, Jonas Noeb & Robert Sulis Ridu (2012). The Bidayuh Language: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow (rev. ed.). SIL e-Book 33. Dallas: SIL International.
new_statements.locator: Part II ch. 4, sec. 4.1.2 'Structure of the ultima', printed p.47 (PDF p.64); also fn. 79, printed p.94 (PDF p.111) and sec. 6.2.4, printed p.292 (PDF p.309)
new_statements.reading: Fixed final (ultima) word stress in citation forms, with enclitics taking the stress when attached; no stress contrast; the penult full/reduced vowel distinction is a historical reflex of PAN accent, not synchronic stress. Bukar-Sadung (Eastern) data are among the examples throughout (e.g. Tebakang, Bunan forms on p.47). The sweep item itself (Rensch 2006 p.2, 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation') says the same in one sentence. Both agree with the catalog's fixed-strict final coding; the only nuance not in the catalog rule is Court's optional secondary stress on the first syllable, which Rensch does not mention.

audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict final stress (rule 01 101 1001...) is supported by four independent statements, three of them verified in held 44 (verbatim; 'oxytone' aside is p.37 not p.38), Rensch et al. 2012:47 (verbatim; also p.94 fn.79, p.292), Rensch 2006:2 (fetched sources now), and Court 1972 via StressTyp2 passage 1441 (verified in StressTyp2.sqlite; original print-only, not held). No source found suggests anything other than final stress; the only nuances are Court's optional secondary stress on the first syllable (catalog rule marks none) and Rensch 2012's note that enclitics take the stress in citation forms vs Court's StressTyp2 forms rəˈminəˌkuʔ with primary on the stem — a domain footnote, not a recode. Not 'well-sourced' only because the lect-specific primary phonology (Court 1966/1972) is held second-hand; optional housekeeping: fix McGinn locator 38 -> 37 and consider promoting Rensc
